metadata.abstract: This study investigated the interplay between intermittent fasting (IF), gut microbiota composition, and systemic inflammation in patients with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). We hypothesized that IF might modulate the abundance of *Clostridium butyricum*, a bacterium associated with gut barrier integrity, and reduce lipopolysaccharide (LPS) levels, a marker of endotoxemia. A randomized controlled trial enrolled 60 participants (30 with AD and 30 with UC) who underwent 12 weeks of IF (alternate-day fasting). Fecal samples were collected at baseline and post-intervention for quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis of *C. butyricum* abundance and LPS gene expression. Serum LPS levels were measured via ELISA. Mann-Whitney U tests compared biomarker changes between groups. Results showed a significant increase in *C. butyricum* abundance (p < 0.01) and a 35% reduction in serum LPS levels (p = 0.02) in the IF group compared to controls. In UC patients, LPS reduction correlated with improved stool consistency (r = -0.43, p = 0.03), while AD patients exhibited lower amyloid-beta levels (p = 0.04). These findings suggest that IF may enhance gut microbiota resilience and mitigate systemic inflammation in comorbid AD/UC, potentially via *C. butyricum*-mediated pathways. Further research is warranted to elucidate mechanistic links and therapeutic applications.

This study investigated the impact of a ketogenic diet on gut microbiota composition, γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels, and symptom severity in human participants with multiple sclerosis (MS) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Twenty adults diagnosed with MS and GERD underwent a 12-week ketogenic diet intervention, with baseline and post-intervention assessments. Ruminococcus gnavus abundance, a gut bacterium linked to inflammatory processes, was quantified via 16S rRNA sequencing. GABA concentrations in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid were measured using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry, while Western blotting analyzed GABA receptor subunit expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests revealed significant increases in R. gnavus abundance (p = 0.012) and plasma GABA levels (p = 0.023) following the diet, alongside trends toward reduced MS-related fatigue and GERD symptom frequency. No adverse effects were reported. Correlation analysis suggested a positive association between R. gnavus abundance and GABA levels (r = 0.47, p = 0.045). These findings suggest that the ketogenic diet may modulate gut microbiota and GABAergic signaling, potentially offering therapeutic benefits for MS and GERD patients. Further research is warranted to elucidate mechanistic pathways and long-term clinical outcomes.

This study investigated the potential therapeutic role of inulin supplementation in modulating gut microbiota and mitigating pathophysiological mechanisms linking amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in C57BL/6 mice. A murine model of ALS combined with GERD was established through genetic manipulation and acid reflux induction. Mice were randomized to receive either inulin or a control diet for 12 weeks. Fecal microbiota composition was analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing a significant enrichment of *Coprococcus comes* in the inulin group (p < 0.01). Butyrate concentrations, measured via gas chromatography, increased by 42% in the inulin group compared to controls (p = 0.003). Flow cytometry analysis of luminal immune cells demonstrated reduced pro-inflammatory macrophage activation (CD11b+ CD86+) and enhanced regulatory T-cell (Treg) frequency in the inulin-treated cohort. Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed statistically significant differences in butyrate levels and immune cell profiles between groups (p < 0.05). Correlation analysis revealed a positive association between *Coprococcus comes* abundance and butyrate production (r = 0.78, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that inulin may alleviate ALS-GERD comorbidity by promoting butyrate-producing bacteria and modulating gut-immune interactions, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigates the interplay between gut microbiota, inflammation, and anxiety-like behaviors in zebrafish models of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Zebrafish were exposed to resistant starch (RS) supplementation to modulate gut microbiota composition. Quantitative PCR was employed to quantify Bifidobacterium adolescentis abundance, a probiotic taxon associated with gut-brain axis regulation. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP), a biomarker of systemic inflammation, was measured alongside anxiety-like behaviors using novel object recognition and light-dark transfer tests. Results revealed RS supplementation significantly increased B. adolescentis colonization (p < 0.05, Mann-Whitney U test) and reduced CRP levels compared to controls. Anxiety-like behaviors were also attenuated in RS-treated fish, correlating with microbiota shifts. These findings suggest that RS-mediated modulation of B. adolescentis may mitigate inflammation and alleviate anxiety symptoms in SIBO-associated GAD. The study highlights the therapeutic potential of prebiotic interventions in disrupting gut-brain axis dysregulation, offering novel insights into microbiota-targeted therapies for neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the potential therapeutic role of probiotic supplementation in mitigating amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) progression in Sprague-Dawley rats with induced small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Rats were randomized to receive either a probiotic containing *Coprococcus comes* or a placebo, alongside standard ALS-inducing protocols. To assess microbial and metabolic alterations, gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) was employed to profile gut-derived metabolites, while interleukin-10 (IL-10) levels were quantified via ELISA to evaluate anti-inflammatory responses. Pearson correlation analyses were conducted to explore relationships between microbial taxa, metabolite profiles, and IL-10 expression. Results revealed that *C. comes* supplementation significantly reduced SIBO severity, as evidenced by decreased bacterial load and altered metabolic signatures, compared to controls. Concurrently, IL-10 levels were markedly elevated in treated rats, correlating positively with reduced motor neuron degeneration. GC-MS identified specific short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites that aligned with anti-inflammatory pathways. These findings suggest that modulating gut microbiota with *C. comes* may alleviate ALS pathology via enhanced IL-10-mediated immunomodulation and metabolic reprogramming. This study highlights the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in neurodegenerative diseases linked to gastrointestinal dysbiosis.

This study investigated the impact of resistant starch supplementation on gut microbiota composition and inflammatory biomarker levels in adults with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 40 participants, who were assigned to receive either 15 g/day of resistant starch or a cellulose placebo for 8 weeks. Fecal samples were analyzed for microbial composition using 16S rRNA sequencing, and serum interleukin-1β (IL-1β) levels were quantified via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Participants also completed symptom severity assessments. Results revealed significant increases in *Bacteroides vulgatus* abundance in the resistant starch group compared to the placebo group (p = 0.012). IL-1β levels decreased by 28% in the intervention group (p = 0.003), while no significant changes were observed in the placebo group. Student’s t-tests confirmed statistically significant differences in both microbial and biomarker outcomes. No adverse effects were reported. These findings suggest that resistant starch may modulate gut microbiota and reduce systemic inflammation in individuals with ASD and GERD, potentially offering a therapeutic strategy for managing comorbid gastrointestinal and neurodevelopmental conditions. Further research is needed to elucidate mechanistic pathways and long-term clinical efficacy.

This study investigated the potential of inulin supplementation to modulate brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels in individuals with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 60 participants, with 30 assigned to receive daily inulin (10 g) and 30 to a placebo for 12 weeks. BDNF concentrations were measured via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) at baseline and post-intervention. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing to assess Lactobacillus plantarum abundance. The Mann-Whitney U test revealed statistically significant increases in BDNF levels in the inulin group compared to the placebo group (p = 0.012), with a median increase of 18.3% (95% CI: 9.1–27.5). Correlation analysis showed a positive association between L. plantarum abundance and BDNF levels (r = 0.42, p = 0.003). No significant differences in GERD symptoms were observed between groups. These findings suggest that inulin-mediated enhancement of L. plantarum may influence BDNF, potentially offering a novel therapeutic strategy for GAD and GERD. Further research is warranted to elucidate mechanistic pathways and long-term effects.

This study investigated the interplay between small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and epilepsy in zebrafish, focusing on the role of *Coprococcus comes* and its modulation by synbiotic supplementation. Zebrafish models with induced SIBO exhibited increased seizure frequency and elevated interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels, suggesting a gut-brain axis link. To explore therapeutic potential, zebrafish were administered a synbiotic containing *Coprococcus comes* and prebiotic fibers. RNA sequencing of brain and intestinal tissues revealed differential expression of immune-related genes, including *il6*, following synbiotic treatment. Spearman correlation analysis demonstrated a significant inverse relationship between *Coprococcus comes* abundance and IL-6 expression (r = -0.72, p < 0.01), alongside reduced seizure activity. Notably, synbiotic intervention restored microbiota diversity and attenuated neuroinflammatory markers, correlating with improved seizure outcomes. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of targeting *Coprococcus comes* through synbiotic supplementation to modulate IL-6-driven inflammation in SIBO-associated epilepsy. The study underscores the gut-brain axis as a critical pathway for neuroprotection, offering novel insights into microbiota-directed therapies for neurological disorders. Results support further investigation of synbiotic interventions in human epilepsy and SIBO comorbidities.

This study investigated the potential therapeutic effects of probiotic supplementation containing *Coprococcus comes* on the comorbidities of major depressive disorder (MDD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in Sprague-Dawley rats. Rats were randomized into two groups: a control group receiving standard chow and a treatment group receiving chow supplemented with *C. comes* for eight weeks. Behavioral assessments using the forced-swim test and open-field test evaluated depressive-like behaviors, while GERD severity was quantified via esophageal pH monitoring and histological analysis of gastric mucosa. Serotonin levels in the hippocampus and colon were measured using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Gut microbiota composition was analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing. Results demonstrated significant reductions in depressive behaviors (p < 0.01) and GERD symptoms (p < 0.05) in the treatment group. LC-MS revealed a 2.3-fold increase in hippocampal serotonin levels (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.01) and enhanced colonic serotonin bioavailability. *C. comes* colonization was significantly elevated in treated rats, correlating with reduced inflammatory markers. These findings suggest that *C. comes*-mediated modulation of serotonin signaling may represent a novel therapeutic strategy for MDD-GERD comorbidities, highlighting the gut-brain axis as a critical pathway for integrative treatment approaches.

This study investigated the interplay between ulcerative colitis (UC), generalized anxiety disorder (GAD), and the gut microbiota in BALB/c mice, with a focus on the therapeutic potential of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT). Mice were divided into groups receiving either donor fecal microbiota enriched with *Roseburia intestinalis* or standard FMT, alongside a control group. Behavioral assessments revealed reduced anxiety-like behaviors in the *Roseburia*-enriched FMT group, correlating with increased brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels in the prefrontal cortex. Concurrently, UC symptoms, as measured by colon histology and cytokine profiles, were significantly attenuated. Gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) analysis identified altered metabolomic signatures, including elevated short-chain fatty acids, in the *Roseburia*-treated group. Principal component analysis (PCA) of combined behavioral, metabolic, and microbiological data revealed distinct clusters associated with microbial composition and neurobehavioral outcomes. These findings suggest that *Roseburia intestinalis* may modulate both intestinal inflammation and anxiety via BDNF-dependent pathways, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for comorbid UC and GAD. The study underscores the gut-brain axis as a critical target for microbiota-based interventions, with potential applications in translational medicine for inflammatory and psychiatric disorders.

This study investigated the impact of intermittent fasting (IF) on the comorbidities of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in Sprague-Dawley rats, with a focus on the role of *Bifidobacterium adolescentis* and acetate metabolism. Male rats were randomly assigned to control or IF groups, with IF defined as 12-hour fasting cycles. GAD was induced via chronic stress, while GERD was modeled using a subcutaneous pyloric ligation. Fecal samples were analyzed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) to quantify acetate levels, and 16S rRNA sequencing identified microbial composition. Behavioral assessments measured anxiety-like behaviors via the elevated plus maze, while GERD severity was evaluated via esophageal pH monitoring. Results revealed that IF significantly reduced anxiety-like behaviors (p < 0.01) and GERD symptoms (p < 0.05) compared to controls. *Bifidobacterium adolescentis* abundance increased by 42% in IF rats, correlating with elevated acetate concentrations (p < 0.001). Student’s t-tests confirmed significant differences in all measured parameters. These findings suggest that IF modulates the gut-brain axis by enhancing *B. adolescentis* and acetate production, offering potential therapeutic strategies for GAD and GERD. This study underscores the interplay between dietary interventions, gut microbiota, and neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, inflammatory biomarkers, and neurological outcomes in individuals with co-occurring epilepsy and Crohn’s disease. A cohort of 50 human participants with confirmed diagnoses of both conditions was enrolled, and 25 received a 4-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics, while 25 received a placebo. Fecal samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing to assess Prevotella copri abundance, and serum interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels were quantified via liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS). Correlation analyses were performed using Spearman’s method to evaluate associations between microbial composition, inflammatory biomarkers, and seizure frequency. Results revealed a significant inverse correlation between P. copri abundance and serum IL-6 levels (r = -0.48, p < 0.01) in the antibiotic group, compared to no significant correlation in the placebo group. Additionally, participants treated with antibiotics exhibited a 32% reduction in seizure frequency, alongside a 27% decrease in IL-6 concentrations. LC-MS analysis identified altered metabolite profiles in antibiotic-treated individuals, including reduced levels of kynurenine pathway intermediates, which are linked to neuroinflammation. These findings suggest that broad-spectrum antibiotics may modulate gut microbiota to suppress systemic inflammation, potentially alleviating both gastrointestinal and neurological symptoms. The study highlights the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted interventions in complex, multi-system disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, Clostridioides difficile infection, and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) in C57BL/6 mice. We hypothesized that resistant starch supplementation could modulate gut microbiota composition, thereby mitigating ASD-like behaviors and restoring dopamine homeostasis. Mice were subjected to C. difficile infection to induce gastrointestinal dysbiosis, followed by resistant starch treatment (2% w/v in drinking water) for 4 weeks. Fecal microbiota analysis revealed a significant increase in Bifidobacterium longum abundance in the treatment group compared to controls (p < 0.01, Mann-Whitney U test). Concurrently, liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) quantified dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex and striatum, showing a 38% elevation in the resistant starch group (p = 0.02). Behavioral assessments using the social interaction test and marble burying assay demonstrated reduced repetitive behaviors and improved social approach in treated mice. Correlation analysis revealed a strong positive association between B. longum abundance and dopamine levels (r = 0.72, p < 0.001). These findings suggest that resistant starch-induced enrichment of B. longum may restore dopaminergic signaling disrupted by C. difficile infection, offering a potential therapeutic avenue for ASD-associated gut-brain axis dysfunction. The study underscores the role of microbiota-modulating interventions in neurodevelopmental disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, dietary intervention, and neurochemical markers in a murine model of Parkinson’s disease (PD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). BALB/c mice with induced IBS and early-stage PD-like symptoms were fed a polyphenol-rich diet (PRD) for eight weeks. The hypothesis was that PRD modulation of Bacteroides vulgatus abundance would influence dopamine metabolism, a key biomarker in PD pathology. Fecal microbiota analysis revealed a 42% increase in B. vulgatus abundance in PRD-fed mice compared to controls (p < 0.01). Western blotting demonstrated elevated tyrosine hydroxylase (TH) expression in midbrain regions of PRD-treated animals, correlating with a 28% rise in striatal dopamine levels (p = 0.003). No significant differences in IBS symptoms were observed between groups, suggesting dietary intervention may target neurodegenerative pathways without exacerbating gastrointestinal dysfunction. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirmed statistically significant changes in dopamine biomarkers and microbiota composition. These findings support a mechanistic link between B. vulgatus, polyphenol metabolism, and dopaminergic homeostasis, offering novel insights into microbiota-directed therapies for PD. The study underscores the potential of dietary interventions to modulate both neurodegenerative and gastrointestinal disorders through microbiota-mediated pathways.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, serotonin levels, and behavioral phenotypes in domestic pigs with induced Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD)-like behaviors and Clostridioides difficile infection. Pigs were administered broad-spectrum antibiotics to disrupt gut microbiota and induce C. difficile colonization. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed significant depletion of Faecalibacterium prausnitzii, a key anti-inflammatory bacterium, alongside increased abundance of pathogenic taxa associated with C. difficile. Serum and fecal serotonin concentrations were measured via high-performance liquid chromatography, revealing a 42% reduction compared to controls. Spearman correlation analysis demonstrated a strong inverse relationship between F. prausnitzii abundance and serotonin levels (r = -0.78, p < 0.001). Behavioral assessments using standardized pig ASD-like behavior scales showed increased repetitive behaviors and social interaction deficits correlating with microbiota and serotonin changes. These findings suggest that broad-spectrum antibiotic-induced dysbiosis disrupts the gut-brain axis via serotonin-mediated pathways, potentially exacerbating ASD-like symptoms. The study highlights F. prausnitzii as a critical mediator of serotonin homeostasis in the gut and underscores the role of microbiota-targeted therapies in mitigating neurodevelopmental disorders. This pig model provides a translational platform for investigating microbiome interventions in human ASD and gastrointestinal infections.

This study investigates the interplay between gut microbiota modulation, epilepsy, and Clostridioides difficile infection in BALB/c mice. Ruminococcus gnavus, a key gut bacterium associated with metabolic and inflammatory processes, was targeted through inulin supplementation, a prebiotic known to selectively enrich gut microbial taxa. Metatranscriptomic sequencing of fecal samples revealed significant shifts in microbial gene expression profiles following inulin treatment. PERMANOVA analysis demonstrated distinct microbiome community structures between groups, with inulin-supplemented mice exhibiting enhanced R. gnavus abundance and elevated butyrate production, a primary biomarker linked to anti-inflammatory and neuroprotective effects. Notably, C. difficile infection severity was reduced in mice receiving inulin, correlating with increased butyrate levels and diminished intestinal inflammation. Epileptic seizure frequency, monitored via electroencephalography, was significantly lower in inulin-treated animals compared to controls, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for microbiota-targeted interventions. These findings highlight the bidirectional relationship between gut microbiota and neurological health, emphasizing the importance of butyrate-producing taxa in modulating both gastrointestinal and neurologic disorders. The study underscores the feasibility of prebiotic-based therapies to mitigate C. difficile-associated complications and reduce epilepsy severity through microbiome-directed mechanisms.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, immune activation, and disease progression in a murine model of multiple sclerosis (MS) exacerbated by *Clostridioides difficile* infection. BALB/c mice were treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics to induce dysbiosis and subsequent *C. difficile* colonization. Subgroup cohorts received oral supplementation of *Bifidobacterium adolescentis* to assess its therapeutic potential. Serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels, a biomarker of systemic inflammation, were quantified via flow cytometry alongside immune cell subsets in the central nervous system. Results demonstrated that antibiotic-induced dysbiosis significantly elevated CRP levels (p < 0.01) and worsened MS severity, as evidenced by increased demyelination and T-cell infiltration. *B. adolescentis* supplementation reversed these effects, reducing CRP by 42% (p < 0.05) and attenuating neuroinflammation. Flow cytometry revealed that *B. adolescentis* modulated CD4+ T-cell subsets, increasing regulatory T-cell (Treg) frequencies and decreasing pro-inflammatory Th17 cells. These findings suggest that *B. adolescentis* may mitigate MS pathogenesis by restoring gut microbiota balance and suppressing systemic inflammation. The study underscores the role of gut microbiota in neuroimmune interactions and highlights potential therapeutic strategies targeting microbiome dysbiosis in MS and *C. difficile*-associated diseases. Student’s t-test was used to analyze statistical significance, with differences considered significant at p < 0.05.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, inflammatory gastrointestinal pathology, and depressive-like behaviors in domestic pigs, focusing on the role of *Prevotella copri* and the impact of broad-spectrum antibiotics. A cohort of pigs with experimentally induced Crohn’s disease-like inflammation was treated with a 14-day course of broad-spectrum antibiotics, while a control group received a placebo. Behavioral assessments using the elevated plus maze and open field test quantified depressive-like symptoms, while serum brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels were measured via ELISA. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and Spearman correlation was employed to assess associations between microbial taxa, BDNF levels, and behavioral outcomes. Results revealed a significant reduction in *P. copri* abundance in antibiotic-treated pigs, correlating with lower serum BDNF levels and increased depressive-like behaviors. Notably, the correlation between *P. copri* abundance and BDNF levels (r = −0.72, p < 0.01) persisted across treatment groups, suggesting a microbiota-brain axis link. These findings highlight *P. copri* as a potential therapeutic target in inflammatory conditions associated with depression, while broad-spectrum antibiotics may disrupt this axis, exacerbating neurobehavioral outcomes. This study underscores the complex relationship between gut microbiota, inflammation, and neuropsychiatric disorders in a translational animal model.

This study investigated the impact of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) enriched with *Lactobacillus plantarum* on Parkinson’s disease (PD) progression in Wistar rats with experimentally induced small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). Rats were divided into groups receiving either FMT with *L. plantarum*-dominant microbiota or sham FMT. PD symptoms were assessed via motor function tests, while SIBO was confirmed through bacterial culturing and 16S rRNA sequencing. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed significant shifts in gut microbiota composition post-FMT, with increased abundance of *L. plantarum* and reduced pathogenic taxa. Butyrate levels, a key metabolite of *L. plantarum*, were measured using gas chromatography and correlated with motor performance. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests demonstrated statistically significant improvements in motor function (p < 0.01) and elevated butyrate concentrations (p < 0.05) in FMT-treated rats compared to controls. Additionally, metagenomic analysis identified enriched pathways related to short-chain fatty acid synthesis and neuroinflammation suppression. These findings suggest that *L. plantarum*-mediated FMT modulates gut microbiota, enhances butyrate production, and mitigates PD-like symptoms in SIBO-associated models. This study highlights the potential of microbiota-targeted therapies in neurodegenerative disorders, emphasizing the gut-brain axis as a therapeutic avenue.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, inflammation, and neurobehavioral outcomes in a mouse model of major depressive disorder (MDD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). C57BL/6 mice were subjected to broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment to disrupt gut microbiota, with a focus on the depletion of *Clostridium butyricum*, a commensal bacterium implicated in gut-brain axis regulation. RNA sequencing was employed to profile transcriptional changes in the colon and prefrontal cortex, while interleukin-1β (IL-1β) levels were quantified in serum and brain tissues. Antibiotic treatment significantly reduced *C. butyricum* abundance and altered microbial diversity, correlating with heightened anxiety-like behaviors and depressive symptoms. RNA sequencing revealed dysregulated pathways in immune response and synaptic plasticity, with IL-1β expression elevated in both gut and brain tissues. Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed statistically significant differences in gene expression across treatment groups, particularly in cytokine signaling and neuroinflammation-related genes. These findings suggest that *C. butyricum* depletion via antibiotics exacerbates inflammation and neurobehavioral deficits, highlighting the gut microbiota’s role in MDD and IBS pathophysiology. The study underscores the potential of microbiota-targeted interventions as therapeutic strategies for comorbid gastrointestinal and neurological disorders.

This study investigates the interplay between gut microbiota, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD), and major depressive disorder (MDD) in BALB/c mice. We hypothesized that broad-spectrum antibiotic-induced dysbiosis would alter microbial composition, exacerbate GERD symptoms, and contribute to MDD-like behaviors. Mice were treated with broad-spectrum antibiotics for 14 days, followed by assessments of GERD severity via esophageal pH monitoring and MDD-like behaviors using the forced swimming test. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed a significant reduction in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance, a keystone species associated with gut health, in antibiotic-treated mice compared to controls (Student’s t-test, p < 0.01). Concurrently, GERD symptoms, including acid reflux frequency, increased by 42% (p < 0.05). Behavioral analysis showed prolonged immobility in antibiotic-treated mice, indicative of depressive-like behavior. γ-Aminobutyric acid (GABA) levels in the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex were reduced by 31% (p < 0.01), correlating with both behavioral and physiological changes. These findings suggest that antibiotic-induced depletion of F. prausnitzii disrupts gut-brain axis function, potentially linking GERD and MDD through altered GABA signaling. This study underscores the role of specific gut microbiota in neuropsychiatric and gastrointestinal pathologies, offering novel insights into therapeutic strategies targeting microbial communities.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, gastrointestinal dysfunction, and anxiety-like behaviors in Sprague-Dawley rats. We hypothesized that perturbations in Collinsella aerofaciens abundance, induced by broad-spectrum antibiotic treatment, would alter acetate production and exacerbate symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). Male rats were divided into groups receiving either vehicle or broad-spectrum antibiotics for 14 days. Anxiety-like behaviors were assessed using the elevated plus maze and open field tests, while GERD symptoms were quantified via esophageal pH monitoring. Fecal microbiota composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing, and acetate levels were measured via gas chromatography. Western blotting was employed to assess expression of corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) and transient receptor potential vanilloid 1 (TRPV1) in the amygdala and esophageal tissues. Kruskal-Wallis tests revealed significant group differences in anxiety scores (p < 0.01) and GERD severity (p < 0.05). Antibiotic treatment reduced C. aerofaciens abundance by 62% and acetate concentrations by 45%, correlating with elevated CRH and TRPV1 expression. These findings suggest that dysbiosis of C. aerofaciens disrupts the gut-brain axis, contributing to GAD and GERD pathogenesis. Targeting this microbial pathway may offer novel therapeutic strategies for co-occurring anxiety and gastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the impact of a polyphenol-rich diet on gut microbiota composition, short-chain fatty acid production, and inflammatory markers in domestic pigs with experimentally induced multiple sclerosis (MS) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Pigs were divided into groups receiving either a standard diet or a polyphenol-enriched diet for 12 weeks. Fecal samples were analyzed using liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry to quantify acetate levels, a primary biomarker of microbial fermentation. 16S rRNA sequencing revealed significant enrichment of *Blautia obeum* in the polyphenol group, correlating with elevated acetate concentrations. PERMANOVA analysis demonstrated distinct microbial community structures between dietary groups, with *Blautia obeum* abundance strongly associated with reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine expression in both MS and UC models. Acetate levels correlated inversely with disease severity scores, suggesting a potential therapeutic role for *Blautia obeum*-mediated metabolic pathways. These findings highlight the interplay between gut microbiota, diet, and neuroinflammation, offering new insights into the gut-brain axis in autoimmune disorders. The study underscores the potential of polyphenol-based interventions to modulate microbial ecology and mitigate systemic inflammation in complex diseases.

This study investigates the interplay between omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, gut microbiota composition, and the pathophysiology of schizophrenia and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) in C57BL/6 mice. Mice were subjected to a GERD-inducing protocol and randomized to receive omega-3 fatty acid supplementation or a vehicle control. Gut microbiota analysis revealed a significant enrichment of *Bifidobacterium longum* in the omega-3 group compared to controls, accompanied by elevated fecal butyrate levels. RNA sequencing of colonic tissue identified differential expression of genes involved in inflammatory response and neurotransmitter synthesis, with notable upregulation of *Il10* and *Gad1* in the supplemented group. Butyrate levels correlated with reduced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines in the hippocampus, suggesting potential neuroprotective effects. Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed statistically significant differences in microbiota composition (p < 0.01) and gene expression (p < 0.05) between groups. These findings highlight the role of *B. longum* and butyrate in modulating gut-brain axis signaling, with omega-3 supplementation potentially mitigating GERD-related inflammation and schizophrenia-associated neurochemical imbalances. This study underscores the therapeutic potential of targeting gut microbiota through dietary interventions in dual neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between intermittent fasting (IF), gut microbiota composition, and metabolic biomarkers in individuals with generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). A randomized controlled trial enrolled 50 human participants, with 25 assigned to an IF intervention (16-hour fasting periods) and 25 to a standard diet. Fecal samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing to assess microbial community structure, while plasma acetate levels were quantified via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Pearson correlation analysis was employed to evaluate associations between microbial taxa, acetate concentrations, and clinical outcomes. Results revealed a significant reduction in *Ruminococcus gnavus* abundance in the IF group compared to controls (p < 0.01), alongside a 22% increase in plasma acetate levels. Correlation analysis demonstrated a strong inverse relationship between *R. gnavus* abundance and anxiety symptom severity (r = -0.68, p < 0.001) and a positive correlation between acetate levels and reduced inflammatory markers (r = 0.55, p = 0.003). These findings suggest that IF may modulate gut microbiota composition and enhance short-chain fatty acid production, potentially mitigating both GAD and UC pathophysiology. The study highlights *R. gnavus* as a candidate therapeutic target and underscores the translational potential of dietary interventions in neuroimmune disorders. Further research is warranted to elucidate mechanistic pathways and optimize intervention protocols.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, stress physiology, and inflammatory processes in patients with comorbid Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) and Crohn’s disease. A cohort of 60 human participants with confirmed diagnoses underwent a 14-day intervention of broad-spectrum antibiotics, with 30 individuals receiving the intervention and 30 serving as untreated controls. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples revealed significant depletion of *Lactobacillus plantarum* in the treatment group, accompanied by a 28% increase in alpha-diversity compared to controls (PERMANOVA, p < 0.01). Concurrently, salivary cortisol levels rose by 19% in the antibiotic group, correlating with heightened inflammatory markers (IL-6 and TNF-α). Notably, participants with pre-existing low *L. plantarum* abundance exhibited a 40% greater cortisol response to the intervention. Multivariate analysis identified *L. plantarum* as a key driver of microbiome stability, with its reduction linked to amplified hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation. These findings suggest that broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the gut-brain axis by altering *L. plantarum* populations, thereby exacerbating stress-related pathophysiology in individuals with MDD and Crohn’s disease. The study underscores the need for targeted antimicrobial stewardship and highlights *L. plantarum* as a potential therapeutic target for mitigating comorbid psychiatric and gastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the potential association between synbiotic supplementation, gut microbiota composition, and inflammatory biomarker levels in patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD) and Crohn’s disease (CD). A cohort of 120 human participants, comprising 60 PD patients and 60 CD patients, received a synbiotic intervention containing *Akkermansia muciniphila*-enriched probiotics and prebiotic fibers for 12 weeks. Fecal samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing to assess microbial diversity, while serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were quantified as a marker of systemic inflammation. Spearman correlation analysis revealed a significant positive association between baseline *A. muciniphila* abundance and reduced CRP levels in CD patients (r = 0.42, p < 0.01), but no significant correlation in PD patients. Post-intervention, *A. muciniphila* abundance increased by 38% in CD participants, correlating with a 22% decrease in CRP (r = 0.39, p = 0.02). In PD patients, no significant changes in *A. muciniphila* or CRP were observed. These findings suggest that synbiotic supplementation may modulate gut microbiota and reduce inflammation in CD, but its efficacy in PD remains unclear. The study highlights the differential role of *A. muciniphila* in inflammatory conditions and underscores the need for targeted microbiota-based therapies for neuroinflammatory and gastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, gut microbiota composition, and metabolic biomarkers in a rat model of migraine and functional dyspepsia. Sprague-Dawley rats were assigned to groups receiving either a standard diet or a diet supplemented with omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA) for eight weeks. Functional dyspepsia was induced via a low-dose chronic stress protocol, while migraine-like symptoms were assessed using the von Frey test and cortical evoked potentials. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed via 16S rRNA sequencing, with a focus on Prevotella copri abundance. Plasma acetate levels were quantified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry, and immune cell activation was evaluated via flow cytometry. Principal component analysis revealed a significant shift in microbial community structure and metabolic profiles in the omega-3-supplemented group, characterized by reduced Prevotella copri abundance and elevated plasma acetate concentrations. Flow cytometry demonstrated decreased CD11b+ macrophage activation and reduced Th17 cell frequencies in the small intestine. Correlation analyses suggested that increased acetate levels and altered microbiota composition were inversely associated with migraine-like behaviors and dyspeptic symptoms. These findings support a potential mechanistic link between omega-3-induced modulation of gut microbiota and metabolic pathways in the pathophysiology of migraine and functional dyspepsia, offering novel therapeutic perspectives for these comorbid conditions.

This study investigates the interplay between ketogenic diet-induced alterations in gut microbiota, short-chain fatty acid production, and neuroinflammatory pathways in a murine model of Alzheimer’s disease and irritable bowel syndrome. BALB/c mice were randomized to receive either a standard chow diet or a ketogenic diet for 12 weeks, with behavioral and histopathological assessments conducted alongside microbiome analysis. Roseburia intestinalis abundance, a key producer of acetate, was significantly elevated in ketogenic diet-fed mice compared to controls, correlating with increased fecal acetate levels. RNA sequencing of gut and hippocampal tissue revealed differential expression of genes involved in neuroinflammation and synaptic plasticity, including IL-6 and BDNF, in ketogenic-fed animals. PERMANOVA analysis confirmed distinct microbial community structures between dietary groups, with Roseburia intestinalis-driven shifts in the gut microbiome associated with reduced amyloid-beta plaque deposition in the hippocampus. These findings suggest that ketogenic diet modulation of Roseburia intestinalis may enhance acetate-mediated neuroprotection, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for dual management of Alzheimer’s disease and irritable bowel syndrome. The study underscores the microbiota-gut-brain axis as a critical target for integrative interventions in neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the potential therapeutic role of a high-fiber diet in modulating gut microbiota and inflammatory biomarkers in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). A randomized controlled trial enrolled 60 human participants, with 30 assigned to a high-fiber diet (containing 30g/day of fermentable fiber) and 30 to a standard diet. Quantitative PCR was used to assess the abundance of *Clostridium butyricum*, a bacterium associated with anti-inflammatory properties, and to measure interleukin-10 (IL-10) expression in peripheral blood mononuclear cells. Principal component analysis revealed a significant correlation between increased *C. butyricum* abundance and elevated IL-10 levels in the high-fiber group compared to controls (p < 0.01). Additionally, participants in the intervention group exhibited reduced systemic inflammation, as indicated by lower levels of pro-inflammatory cytokines. The findings suggest that dietary fiber may enhance the gut microbiota’s capacity to produce anti-inflammatory metabolites, potentially mitigating neuroinflammation in ALS. These results highlight the therapeutic potential of microbiota-targeted dietary interventions in neurodegenerative diseases, warranting further exploration of gut-brain axis modulation in clinical settings.

This study investigates the interplay between traumatic brain injury (TBI) and celiac disease in zebrafish, exploring the therapeutic potential of fecal microbiota transplantation (FMT) enriched with *Bifidobacterium adolescentis*. TBI and celiac disease are linked by shared inflammatory pathways, yet their co-occurrence remains underexplored. Zebrafish were subjected to controlled TBI and induced celiac-like symptoms via dietary gluten exposure. FMT was administered to assess its capacity to modulate neuroinflammation and gastrointestinal pathology. Plasma and brain tissue samples were analyzed for propionate levels, a short-chain fatty acid with neuroprotective properties, using gas chromatography. Western blotting revealed reduced phosphorylated NF-κB and increased cleaved caspase-3 in FMT-treated groups, indicating attenuated inflammation and apoptosis. Principal coordinates analysis (PCoA) of 16S rRNA sequencing demonstrated distinct microbial community shifts in FMT recipients, characterized by elevated *B. adolescentis* abundance. Correlation analysis showed a positive link between propionate concentrations and reduced neuronal damage markers. These findings suggest that *B. adolescentis*-mediated FMT may mitigate TBI-induced neuroinflammation and celiac-associated intestinal dysbiosis through propionate-driven metabolic pathways. This study highlights the translational potential of microbiota modulation in neurogastrointestinal disorders, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for dual-pathology conditions.

This study investigates the interplay between dietary intervention, gut microbiota composition, and neuroinflammatory biomarkers in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and ulcerative colitis (UC). A cohort of 120 human participants with ALS or UC was randomized to either a Mediterranean diet (MD) or a control diet for 12 weeks. Gut microbiota was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, while plasma dopamine levels were quantified via HPLC. Spearman correlation analysis revealed a significant positive association between increased abundance of Coprococcus comes and elevated dopamine concentrations (r = 0.42, p < 0.01) in the MD group. Participants adhering to the MD exhibited greater microbial diversity and higher relative abundance of Coprococcus comes compared to controls (p < 0.05). Notably, dopamine levels correlated inversely with disease severity metrics in ALS patients (r = -0.38, p = 0.02) and UC activity scores (r = -0.35, p = 0.03). Multivariate analysis suggested that Coprococcus comes mediated the diet-induced modulation of dopamine, potentially through short-chain fatty acid production. These findings highlight a potential therapeutic avenue for managing neuroinflammation via microbiota-targeted dietary interventions. The study underscores the role of gut-brain axis interactions in neurodegenerative and inflammatory disorders, offering novel insights into the mechanistic links between diet, microbiota, and neurochemical biomarkers.

This study investigated the interplay between autism spectrum disorder (ASD), irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), and gut microbiota in Wistar rats, focusing on the impact of a ketogenic diet (KD) on Parabacteroides distasonis abundance and systemic inflammation. Male Wistar rats were assigned to either a standard chow diet or a KD for 12 weeks, with behavioral and gastrointestinal symptoms assessed alongside microbiota composition and biomarker levels. Parabacteroides distasonis, a gut bacterium implicated in neuroinflammation, was quantified via 16S rRNA sequencing. C-reactive protein (CRP), a marker of systemic inflammation, was measured using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA). Pearson correlation analysis revealed a significant positive association between Parabacteroides distasonis abundance and CRP levels (r = 0.72, p < 0.01) in KD-fed rats, compared to control groups. Concurrently, KD altered gut microbiota diversity, correlating with reduced repetitive behaviors and improved gastrointestinal motility in ASD-like models. Notably, CRP levels inversely correlated with Parabacteroides distasonis abundance (r = −0.68, p < 0.05), suggesting a potential regulatory role of this bacterium in inflammation. These findings highlight the KD’s capacity to modulate gut microbiota and inflammatory biomarkers, offering novel insights into the bidirectional gut-brain axis in ASD and IBS. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions in managing comorbid neurological and gastrointestinal conditions through microbiota-mediated mechanisms.

This study investigated the interplay between intermittent fasting (IF), gut microbiota composition, and neuroinflammatory biomarkers in patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and celiac disease. Human participants with both conditions underwent a 12-week IF regimen, alternating between 16-hour fasting and 8-hour feeding windows. Fecal microbiota analysis revealed a significant 32% increase in Faecalibacterium prausnitzii abundance compared to baseline (p=0.012, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), correlating with reduced systemic inflammation. Cortisol levels, measured via salivary assays, demonstrated a 19% decline during fasting periods (p=0.037), suggesting enhanced stress resilience. Western blotting analysis of cerebrospinal fluid samples showed downregulation of NF-κB and TNF-α proteins, consistent with anti-inflammatory effects. Notably, participants with higher baseline F. prausnitzii levels exhibited greater cortisol suppression and improved neurocognitive metrics. These findings suggest that IF may modulate gut microbiota and neuroinflammatory pathways in dual-diagnosis patients, potentially offering a non-pharmacological therapeutic strategy. The study underscores the role of F. prausnitzii as a biomarker for metabolic resilience and highlights the need for personalized dietary interventions in neurogastrointestinal disorders. Results support further exploration of microbiota-targeted therapies in ALS and celiac disease management.

This study investigated the association between resistant starch supplementation, gut microbiota composition, and inflammatory biomarkers in individuals with co-occurring major depressive disorder (MDD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). A randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 60 participants, with 30 assigned to receive daily resistant starch supplementation and 30 receiving a placebo over 12 weeks. Fecal samples were collected at baseline and post-intervention for RNA sequencing to assess microbiota gene expression, while serum C-reactive protein (CRP) levels were quantified as a marker of systemic inflammation. The primary bacterial taxon, *Escherichia coli*, exhibited significant changes in abundance and gene expression in the intervention group compared to controls, as determined by RNA sequencing. Mann-Whitney U tests revealed a statistically significant reduction in CRP levels in the resistant starch group (p = 0.023), alongside increased expression of genes related to short-chain fatty acid production and anti-inflammatory pathways. Correlation analyses suggested a link between *E. coli* transcriptomic shifts and CRP modulation. These findings support the hypothesis that resistant starch may alter gut microbial metabolism, reducing systemic inflammation and potentially alleviating symptoms of MDD and IBS. The study highlights the therapeutic potential of dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota in neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigates the potential therapeutic role of inulin supplementation in modulating gut microbiota and neurobiological markers in individuals with co-occurring major depressive disorder (MDD) and celiac disease. A randomized, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 60 adults diagnosed with both conditions, who received either inulin (10 g/day) or a placebo for 12 weeks. Fecal samples were analyzed for Roseburia intestinalis abundance using 16S rRNA sequencing, while plasma brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) levels were quantified via Western blotting. Spearman correlation analyses revealed a significant positive association between Roseburia intestinalis abundance and plasma BDNF levels (r = 0.42, p < 0.01) in the inulin group, but not in the placebo group. Additionally, participants in the inulin group exhibited a 22% increase in Roseburia intestinalis compared to baseline, alongside a 15% rise in BDNF levels, correlating with reduced depressive symptom severity as measured by the Montgomery-Åsberg Depression Rating Scale. These findings suggest that inulin may enhance BDNF production via microbiota-mediated mechanisms, offering a potential adjunct therapy for MDD in celiac disease patients. The study underscores the gut-brain axis as a viable target for integrative treatment strategies in complex neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between dietary intervention, gut microbiota composition, and inflammatory biomarkers in a zebrafish model of schizophrenia and functional dyspepsia. Zebrafish were fed a Mediterranean diet (rich in omega-3 fatty acids, polyphenols, and fiber) or a control diet for eight weeks. Gut microbiota composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA sequencing, revealing a significant enrichment of *Bifidobacterium adolescentis* in the Mediterranean diet group. Liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) identified altered levels of short-chain fatty acids and tryptophan metabolites, which correlated with behavioral and gastrointestinal phenotypes. Plasma interleukin-10 (IL-10), an anti-inflammatory cytokine, was measured via ELISA, showing a 32% increase in the Mediterranean diet group compared to controls. Spearman correlation analysis revealed a strong positive relationship between *B. adolescentis* abundance and IL-10 levels (r = 0.78, p < 0.001), while negative correlations were observed between *B. adolescentis* and markers of gut permeability. These findings suggest that the Mediterranean diet modulates gut microbiota and inflammatory pathways, potentially offering therapeutic potential for schizophrenia and functional dyspepsia. The study highlights the role of diet in shaping microbiome-immune interactions, providing a preclinical framework for translational research in neurogastroenterology.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota dysregulation, stress hormone dynamics, and neuroinflammation in a porcine model of comorbid Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Domestic pigs were selectively bred to exhibit features of both conditions, and then subjected to a 4-week course of broad-spectrum antibiotics to assess microbiome perturbation. 16S rRNA gene sequencing revealed significant depletion of *Prevotella copri*, a bacterium previously implicated in UC pathogenesis, alongside an overrepresentation of opportunistic pathogens in antibiotic-treated groups. Concurrently, plasma cortisol levels—measured via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay—showed a 38% elevation compared to controls, correlating with increased hippocampal inflammation and amyloid-beta plaque accumulation. Mann-Whitney U tests confirmed statistically significant differences in microbial alpha-diversity (p < 0.01) and cortisol concentrations (p < 0.05) between treatment and control cohorts. Notably, *P. copri* abundance inversely correlated with cortisol levels (r = -0.67, p < 0.01), suggesting a potential regulatory role in stress response modulation. These findings highlight the microbiome’s dual influence on gut and brain pathology, underscoring the need for targeted interventions to mitigate antibiotic-induced dysbiosis in complex disease states. The study provides a novel framework for understanding cross-organ system interactions in inflammatory and neurodegenerative disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between diet, gut microbiota, and neurobehavioral outcomes in zebrafish models of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and Crohn’s disease. Zebrafish were subjected to a polyphenol-rich diet to assess its impact on gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed significant enrichment of *Coprococcus comes* in the gut microbiota of dietary-treated fish compared to controls. Propionate, a short-chain fatty acid produced by *C. comes*, was identified as a primary biomarker using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry. Behavioral assays demonstrated reduced anxiety-like behaviors in polyphenol-fed fish, correlating with elevated propionate levels. Concurrently, inflammatory markers in the gut were suppressed, suggesting anti-inflammatory effects of the diet. Statistical analysis using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirmed significant differences in microbial abundance and propionate concentrations between treatment and control groups (p < 0.05). Mechanistic insights suggested that propionate modulated gut-brain signaling via the vagus nerve, potentially mitigating anxiety and inflammation. These findings highlight the role of *C. comes* and dietary polyphenols in shaping gut microbiota and neurobehavioral health, offering a novel therapeutic avenue for GAD and Crohn’s disease. The study underscores the translational potential of microbiota-targeted interventions in dual gastrointestinal-neurological disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between diet, gut microbiota composition, and neurobehavioral outcomes in a zebrafish model of celiac disease and schizophrenia-like behaviors. Zebrafish were fed either a standard diet or a polyphenol-rich diet for eight weeks, with celiac disease induced via a gluten-containing diet. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed significant enrichment of *Bacteroides vulgatus* in the polyphenol group, correlating with reduced intestinal inflammation markers. Cortisol levels, measured via enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, were 32% lower in polyphenol-fed fish compared to controls, with Pearson correlation analysis identifying a strong inverse relationship between *B. vulgatus* abundance and cortisol concentrations (r = -0.78, p < 0.001). Behavioral assessments using open-field and novel tank tests showed reduced anxiety-like behaviors in polyphenol-treated fish, coinciding with increased social interaction time. Notably, *B. vulgatus* gene clusters involved in short-chain fatty acid production were upregulated, suggesting a potential mechanism linking dietary polyphenols to stress modulation. These findings highlight the role of *B. vulgatus* in mediating the gut-brain axis in celiac disease-associated schizophrenia, offering novel insights into microbiome-directed therapies for neurodevelopmental disorders. The study underscores the translational potential of zebrafish models in unraveling complex host-microbe interactions.

This study investigated the impact of a polyphenol-rich diet on gut microbiota composition and metabolic profiles in Wistar rats with induced autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and ulcerative colitis (UC). Animals were randomized to receive either a standard chow diet or a polyphenol-enriched diet for eight weeks. Fecal samples were analyzed using shotgun metagenomic sequencing to assess microbial taxa, with a focus on Coprococcus comes, a bacterium implicated in gut-brain axis modulation. Acetate concentrations were quantified via gas chromatography-mass spectrometry as a primary biomarker of microbial metabolic activity. Behavioral assessments using the open field and social interaction tests evaluated ASD-like phenotypes, while colonic histology and inflammation markers (IL-6, TNF-α) were measured to assess UC progression. Shotgun sequencing revealed significant enrichment of Coprococcus comes in the polyphenol group compared to controls (p < 0.01), accompanied by a 2.3-fold increase in acetate levels (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p < 0.05). Behavioral analyses showed reduced repetitive behaviors and improved social interaction in polyphenol-fed rats, correlating with decreased colonic inflammation. These findings suggest that polyphenol-mediated enhancement of Coprococcus comes and acetate production may modulate ASD and UC pathophysiology via microbiome-gut-brain axis interactions, offering potential therapeutic strategies for comorbid conditions.

This study investigates the interplay between ketogenic diet (KD)-induced metabolic shifts, small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO), and serotonin signaling in domestic pigs with epilepsy. Pigs were assigned to either a standard chow diet or KD for 12 weeks, with SIBO confirmed via lactulose hydrogen breath testing. Fecal microbiota analysis revealed increased abundance of *Bifidobacterium longum* in KD-fed pigs, correlating with reduced SIBO severity. Serotonin levels in hippocampal tissue and plasma were quantified using ELISA, while Western blotting assessed expression of tryptophan hydroxylase-2 (TPH2), the rate-limiting enzyme for serotonin synthesis. Principal component analysis (PCA) of metabolomic and microbiomic data identified distinct metabolic profiles between groups, with KD-associated changes in branched-chain amino acids and short-chain fatty acids further modulating TPH2 activity. Correlation analysis highlighted a bidirectional relationship between *B. longum* abundance and hippocampal serotonin receptor expression, suggesting microbiota-mediated modulation of neurochemical pathways. Results indicate that KD may alleviate epilepsy via microbiota-driven regulation of serotonin homeostasis, offering novel insights into gut-brain axis interventions for neurologic disorders. These findings underscore the potential of dietary strategies to mitigate SIBO and epilepsy through targeted modulation of gut microbiota and neurotransmitter signaling.

This study investigated the impact of a Mediterranean diet on gut microbiota composition and inflammatory biomarker levels in Wistar rats with induced Alzheimer’s disease and celiac disease. Rats were divided into groups receiving either a standard chow diet or a Mediterranean diet enriched with olive oil, nuts, and fermented vegetables. Fecal samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing to assess microbial diversity, with Akkermansia muciniphila abundance as a primary focus. Plasma interleukin-6 (IL-6) levels were quantified via ELISA to evaluate systemic inflammation. Statistical analyses incorporated false discovery rate correction to account for multiple comparisons. Results revealed a significant increase in Akkermansia muciniphila abundance in the Mediterranean diet group compared to controls, accompanied by a 42% reduction in IL-6 levels (p < 0.01). Alpha and beta diversity analyses indicated enhanced microbial stability and shifts toward anti-inflammatory taxa in the intervention group. Correlation analyses further linked higher Akkermansia levels to lower IL-6 concentrations, suggesting a potential mechanistic role in mitigating neuroinflammation and intestinal permeability. These findings support the hypothesis that dietary interventions targeting gut microbiota may offer therapeutic potential for dual neurological and gastrointestinal pathologies. The study underscores the importance of microbiome modulation in disease management and highlights the Mediterranean diet as a promising candidate for translational research.

This study investigates the interplay between broad-spectrum antibiotic-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, *Clostridioides difficile* infection, and migraine-like behaviors in BALB/c mice. Mice were treated with a combination of amoxicillin and clindamycin to induce microbiota disruption, followed by *C. difficile* infection. Metatranscriptomic sequencing of fecal samples revealed significant depletion of *Lactobacillus plantarum* and upregulation of inflammatory pathways, including interleukin-6 (IL-6) signaling, in antibiotic-treated mice compared to controls. Behavioral assays demonstrated increased nociceptive responses, mimicking migraine-like symptoms, in mice with elevated IL-6 levels. The Wilcoxon signed-rank test confirmed statistically significant differences in IL-6 expression (p < 0.01) and microbial gene abundance between pre- and post-intervention groups. Notably, *L. plantarum* depletion correlated with heightened IL-6 production and exacerbated migraine-like behaviors, suggesting a mechanistic link between gut microbiota composition and neuroinflammation. These findings highlight the role of antibiotic-induced dysbiosis in exacerbating both gastrointestinal and neurological pathologies, offering potential therapeutic targets through microbiota modulation. The study underscores the importance of preserving beneficial taxa like *L. plantarum* to mitigate systemic inflammatory responses and prevent neurobehavioral sequelae associated with antibiotic use.

This study investigated the interplay between traumatic brain injury (TBI) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) in Sprague-Dawley rats, focusing on the role of *Escherichia coli* and probiotic supplementation. TBI was induced via controlled cortical impact, and IBS-like symptoms were modeled through dietary manipulation. Rats were randomized to receive either a *E. coli* Nissle 1917-based probiotic or a placebo for 14 days post-injury. RNA sequencing was performed on gut and brain tissues to identify transcriptomic changes, while dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex and colon were quantified via high-performance liquid chromatography. False discovery rate correction was applied to all statistical analyses. Results revealed that probiotic supplementation significantly reduced TBI-induced neuronal damage and attenuated IBS symptoms, as evidenced by improved motor function and reduced visceral hypersensitivity. RNA sequencing identified differential expression of genes related to neuroinflammation, gut barrier integrity, and dopaminergic signaling. Notably, dopamine levels in the prefrontal cortex increased by 32% in probiotic-treated rats compared to controls. Pathway analysis highlighted the modulation of *E. coli*-associated metabolic pathways and downregulation of pro-inflammatory cytokines. These findings suggest that *E. coli* probiotics may restore gut-brain axis homeostasis by enhancing dopamine availability and modulating gene expression, offering a potential therapeutic strategy for comorbid TBI and IBS. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of microbiome-targeted interventions in neurogastrointestinal disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, inflammation, and neurobehavioral outcomes in zebrafish models of generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). Using broad-spectrum antibiotics to disrupt microbial communities, we assessed the impact on Ruminococcus gnavus abundance and its correlation with tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) levels. Zebrafish were exposed to antibiotics for 14 days, followed by behavioral assays for anxiety-like behaviors and histological analysis of intestinal inflammation. Western blotting revealed a significant elevation in TNF-α expression in antibiotic-treated groups compared to controls, alongside a marked reduction in R. gnavus abundance. PERMANOVA analysis confirmed distinct microbial community structures between treatment groups, with R. gnavus exhibiting the strongest association with TNF-α levels. Behavioral testing demonstrated increased anxiety-like behaviors in antibiotic-treated fish, correlating with elevated TNF-α and disrupted gut microbiota. These findings suggest that R. gnavus modulates inflammatory pathways and neurobehavioral outcomes in zebrafish, highlighting its potential role as a therapeutic target for GAD and IBS. The study underscores the bidirectional relationship between gut microbiota and neurogastrointestinal disorders, offering novel insights into microbiome-based interventions for anxiety and inflammatory bowel conditions.

This study investigated the potential therapeutic effects of resistant starch supplementation on generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) in individuals with small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO). A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 60 participants with confirmed SIBO and comorbid GAD. Participants received either 20g/day of resistant starch or a placebo for eight weeks. Fecal samples were analyzed using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS) to quantify propionate, a short-chain fatty acid linked to neuroinflammation and anxiety. The primary bacterial taxon, *Clostridium butyricum*, was assessed via 16S rRNA sequencing. Statistical analysis employed false discovery rate correction to account for multiple comparisons. Results showed a significant increase in *C. butyricum* abundance (p < 0.01) and propionate concentrations (p < 0.05) in the resistant starch group compared to placebo. Correlation analysis revealed a moderate inverse relationship between propionate levels and GAD symptom severity (r = -0.42, p < 0.05). No adverse effects were reported. These findings suggest that resistant starch may modulate gut microbiota and reduce GAD symptoms via propionate-mediated mechanisms, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for SIBO-associated anxiety. Further research is warranted to elucidate causal pathways and optimize dosing regimens.

This study investigated the interplay between gut microbiota, neuroinflammation, and comorbid epilepsy-functional dyspepsia in Sprague-Dawley rats. Rats were assigned to three groups: control (standard diet), antibiotic-treated (broad-spectrum antibiotics for 14 days), and microbiota-reconstituted (antibiotics followed by fecal transplantation). RNA sequencing of gut and hippocampal tissues revealed significant dysbiosis in the antibiotic group, characterized by reduced Prevotella copri abundance and altered expression of genes involved in inflammatory pathways. Interleukin-10 (IL-10) levels in plasma and brain tissue were inversely correlated with microbial shifts, with the antibiotic group showing a 42% decrease in IL-10 compared to controls (p < 0.01). Functional dyspepsia symptoms, assessed via gastric emptying and motility tests, were exacerbated in antibiotic-treated rats, while seizure frequency increased by 31% (p < 0.05). Kruskal-Wallis tests confirmed significant differences in microbial composition (p < 0.001) and gene expression profiles across groups. These findings suggest that broad-spectrum antibiotics disrupt the gut-brain axis by reducing IL-10 and altering Prevotella copri, thereby aggravating both neurological and gastrointestinal disorders. The study highlights the critical role of microbiota in modulating inflammation and disease progression, offering potential therapeutic targets for comorbid epilepsy and functional dyspepsia.

This study investigated the interplay between Clostridioides difficile infection, probiotic supplementation, and epilepsy in Wistar rats, focusing on the role of Bacteroides vulgatus and its metabolite indole-3-propionic acid (IPA). Rats were subjected to C. difficile infection to induce gut dysbiosis and subsequent neurological perturbations, followed by probiotic supplementation with a B. vulgatus-enriched strain. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing revealed significant alterations in gut microbiota composition, with B. vulgatus abundance inversely correlated with seizure frequency. Serum IPA levels, measured via LC-MS/MS, were elevated in probiotic-treated groups compared to controls, suggesting a potential neuroprotective role for this short-chain fatty acid. Spearman correlation analysis demonstrated a strong positive association between B. vulgatus abundance and IPA concentrations (r = 0.78, p < 0.01), while IPA levels correlated inversely with seizure severity (r = -0.65, p < 0.05). Electrophysiological recordings confirmed reduced neuronal hyperexcitability in probiotic-treated rats, aligning with microbiota-derived metabolite modulation. These findings suggest that B. vulgatus-mediated production of IPA may mitigate epilepsy through gut-brain axis mechanisms, offering a novel therapeutic strategy for C. difficile-associated neurological complications. The study underscores the therapeutic potential of targeted probiotic interventions in restoring microbial balance and neurophysiological stability in dysbiosis-related disorders.

This study investigated the interplay between omega-3 fatty acid supplementation, gut microbiota composition, and neuroinflammatory pathways in a murine model of Alzheimer’s disease and Crohn’s disease. BALB/c mice were subjected to omega-3 fatty acid supplementation (eicosapentaenoic acid and docosahexaenoic acid) for 12 weeks, alongside a diet-induced colitis model to mimic Crohn’s disease. RNA sequencing was performed on gut and hippocampal tissues to assess transcriptomic changes, while interleukin-10 (IL-10) levels were quantified via ELISA. Results revealed a significant increase in *Bifidobacterium adolescentis* abundance in the gut microbiota of supplemented mice, correlating with elevated IL-10 production. RNA-seq analysis identified dysregulated pathways in the hippocampus, including reduced expression of pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., TNF-α, IL-6) and upregulated genes involved in synaptic plasticity. Pearson correlation analysis demonstrated a strong inverse relationship between *B. adolescentis* abundance and neuroinflammatory markers, while IL-10 levels positively correlated with gut microbiota diversity. These findings suggest that omega-3 supplementation may modulate the gut-brain axis by enhancing IL-10-mediated anti-inflammatory responses and restoring microbial balance, offering potential therapeutic implications for dual neurogastrointestinal disorders. The study underscores the role of microbiota-targeted interventions in mitigating comorbid conditions.
